questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a squared loss punishes outliers
questions.stem: Explain why squaring errors makes a single far-off prediction dominate the total loss.

answer.exemplar: Squaring turns a large residual into a much larger value, so one far-off point contributes disproportionately to the total. Smaller errors contribute relatively little, so the fit chases outliers.

questions.explanation: Squaring amplifies large residuals, so a single far-off point can dominate the sum. The model then prioritises reducing that one error over fitting the bulk of the data.
questions.hint: Compare the square of a large residual with a small one.

questions.topic: Why an absolute loss is robust
questions.stem: An astronomer predicts meteor counts; one night has an extreme outlier. Why is mean absolute error less affected than mean squared error?

options.text: It uses the median of errors
It grows linearly with error size

questions.explanation: Absolute loss grows linearly, so an outlier adds proportionally rather than quadratically. Squared loss would let that one night dominate the total. MAE does not ignore large errors; it weights them less aggressively.
questions.hint: Compare linear versus quadratic growth of an error.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A classifier predicts 95 of 100 stars as non-variable and 5 as variable. True labels: 90 non-variable, 10 variable. What is accuracy?
questions.explanation: Correct predictions: 90 non-variable plus 0 variable = 90? Wait 5 predicted variable, none correct if all 10 variable missed, so 90 correct out of 100 = 0.90. Recompute: predicted 95 non-variable, 90 true non-variable, so 5 false negatives; predicted 5 variable, 0 true variable, so 5 false positives. Correct = 90 non-variable correct + 0 variable correct = 90, accuracy 0.90.
questions.hint: Count correct predictions over all rows.

questions.stem: Why can a single accuracy score hide poor performance on a rare class?

answer.exemplar: Accuracy weights every row equally, so a model that always predicts the majority class can score high while never detecting the rare class. The score hides the failure because the rare rows are few.

questions.explanation: When one class dominates, a trivial majority predictor looks accurate. The score conceals failure on the minority class because those rows are too few to move the average.

questions.stem: Two positives rank 3rd and 5th among 6 items; two negatives rank 1st, 2nd, 4th, 6th? Recompute: with 2 positives and 4 negatives, pairs=8; positive ranks sum=8, AUC=(8-3)/8=0.625. What is AUC?
